transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-14
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Maya Rivera (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Patel (CTO, Lodestar), Samir Rao (Head of Infra, Lodestar), Elena Voss (Compliance, Lodestar)
Links shared: https://redwood.internal/security-arch.pdf (reference diagram), https://app.redwood/example/pilot-sow (pilot SOW draft)

Summary: quick run-through of Lodestar's internal network segmentation requirements for private deployment. Focus on ingress/egress controls, RBAC/SSO integration, audit log retention/forwarding, and KMS/HSM encryption key management. Agreed to follow up with diagrams and an on-prem lab session.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): All right, thanks everyone for joining, uh, we'll just do quick intros then jump into the network layout that Lodestar provided. Maya and I will lead the technical bits.
[00:14] Priya (CTO): Thanks Alex. We have Samir and Elena on the call, Samir runs infra, Elena handles compliance for PHI and EU residency.
[00:23] Maya (Redwood SE): Great, I pulled the topology that Samir uploaded, trying to reconcile a couple of things — you have a hybrid set up with on-prem core and VPC in AWS us-west-2, is that right?
[00:31] Samir (Lodestar): Yeah, correct. On-prem in their main data center and us-west-2 for burst; we also have a colo footprint in FRA for EU data, but most of the patient data is routed to the on-prem cluster first.
[00:45] Elena (Compliance): Just to be clear, anything classified as PHI must remain in EU or our on-prem facilities unless we get explicit consent and contractual addendum.
[00:55] Alex: Understood. We're going to talk private deployment options — VPC peering, private endpoints, and the on-prem air-gapped packaging. We'll also cover how audit logs and key management work.
[01:10] Maya: First question on segmentation — do you currently run micro-segmentation inside the on-prem cluster (e.g., L3 ACLs, or do you do host-based like iptables)?
[01:18] Samir: It's a mix, right now we have VLAN-based segmentation and iptables rules on the app hosts. We're evaluating eBPF for finer-grained policies but haven't rolled it out.
[01:28] Maya: OK, that aligns with what we've seen. Redwood's private package supports deploying a lightweight network-proxy inside the VPC that terminates clients to private endpoints; for on-prem we recommend a dedicated network zone with strict ACLs, no direct internet egress from the inference hosts.
[01:42] Priya: When you say no direct internet egress, do you mean all egress has to go via a NAT/proxy that you control? We need to ensure updates and metrics can still go out.
[01:50] Maya: Yes: typically you have an egress gateway — e.g., NAT plus an egress proxy that logs requests. For SaaS telemetry we can route through a managed egress proxy in the customer account or via a controlled outbound path that enforces TLS inspection and logging.
[02:05] Samir: We need to ensure that the outbound IPs are fixed for firewall allow-lists. We can't have ephemeral ranges.
[02:11] Alex: For Dedicated/Private we publish static egress IPs per region or we can set up NAT in your VPC with Elastic IPs. For on-prem we can do a reverse-proxy model where you punch an outbound tunnel to Redwood control plane — all traffic is over mTLS and originates from your IPs.
[02:27] Elena: Audit logs — how granular are they? We need request-level logs for model invocations, user/team identifiers, timestamps, and redaction markers for PHI. Also chain-of-custody for who accessed keys.
[02:40] Maya: We capture token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and we can emit per-request metadata to your SIEM via syslog or a cloud log sink. For PHI redaction we support programmable hooks so sensitive fields can be masked before logs are forwarded.
[02:54] Priya: What about retention? Regulator wants 7 years for certain audit trails.
[02:59] Alex: We can hold logs in your account for arbitrary retention windows; for Hosted customers we typically default to 90 days but on Private we mirror to your S3/LOB where you control lifecycle policies.
[03:12] Samir: KMS — we operate Cloud KMS and have our own HSM for highest-sensitivity keys. How would Redwood integrate?
[03:19] Maya: We support customer-managed keys in major cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Google KMS) and HSM-backed keys via token or external key manager. For on-prem we can integrate with your HSM over a network KMIP interface or use an offline-wrap model for keys.
[03:33] Priya: Is the model weights encrypted at rest in your runtime?
[03:37] Maya: Yes — models at rest are encrypted with keys you control. In memory we minimize plaintext exposure, and we purge KV caches between sessions where required. There is also an option for application-level crypto using enclave-like protections for extra-sensitive workloads.
[03:52] Elena: We need a statement for SOC2 and ISO mapping: does Redwood's Private control plane produce evidence for logs and rotation?
[03:59] Alex: We have an enterprise pack: SOC 2 coverage for the control plane, and for Private deployments we provide a compliance bundle — config manifests, rotation schedules, and an audit playbook. We'll share the SOC 2 attestation and the ISO alignment doc after the call.
[04:15] Maya: On network hardening: recommended inbound model — completely private, no public ELBs. Use VPC endpoints or private DNS, and zero trust between subnets with RBAC enforced at the application layer.
[04:30] Samir: How do you handle cross-account peering? We prefer not to peer accounts, we want cross-account deployments with least privileges.
[04:37] Maya: We can run in your account or we can deploy in a partner account with cross-account roles. For VPC connectivity we recommend AWS PrivateLink/Interface endpoints instead of peering when you need strict isolation and controlled egress.
[04:52] Dr. Patel: We also have an on-prem staging cluster in an air-gapped environment for PHI testing. Can the private package be air-gapped?
[04:58] Alex: Yes, we have an on-prem bundle that can be installed without outbound connectivity except initial attestation. It uses signed images and optional offline key provisioning. Maintenance is via signed patches you pull into a staging repo.
[05:12] Elena: For SSO and RBAC, we use SAML2 via Okta. We need audit trails for admin actions, and SCIM provisioning if possible.
[05:21] Maya: We integrate with SAML/Okta for user auth and SCIM for provisioning. Admin actions are emitted to audit logs with who/when/what; we also support attribute-based access controls (ABAC) for fine-grained policy.
[05:34] Samir: One of our concerns is lateral movement if an app host is compromised. How do you limit the blast radius?
[05:41] Maya: Limit by network zones + host-level protections. We deploy sidecars that enforce egress only to authorized services, mTLS for service-to-service, and ephemeral credentials via short-lived certs. Also guardrails in the runtime to prevent arbitrary outbound sockets from model processes.
[06:01] Alex: Let's look at the diagram Samir sent — Maya, can you pull it up?
[06:10] Maya: (screen share) I see the colo in FRA, on-prem core, and two VPCs in us-west-2. You've got an open NAT gateway for some subnets — that's a big egress surface. Recommend a dedicated egress VPC with logging and WAF if you need to filter endpoints.
[06:31] Samir: Right now, dev subnet has a direct route to internet for package pulls. We want to lock prod.
[06:38] Maya: For prod inference hosts we recommend no internet route, packages should be pulled via an internal artifact repo that syncs from a controlled upstream. We'll provide an ops runbook for locking down iptables + a sample iptables rule-set.
[06:51] Elena: On the audit playbook, can you show chain-of-custody for keys? We need to know key rotation cadence and access logs.
[06:59] Maya: Example: AWS KMS key with automatic rotation every 365 days, access via IAM roles, CloudTrail for key usage. For HSM we log KMIP operations and can forward to your SIEM. We'll include sample CloudTrail queries in the docs.
[07:14] Priya: We also need to know failure modes: if your control plane is unreachable, can inference continue locally?
[07:21] Alex: For Private on-prem we support local-only mode: inference runtime can operate offline with pinned model versions; control-plane features like rollouts are paused but serving continues. We also have TTL caches to avoid re-fetching model artifacts.
[07:35] Samir: What about egress filtering at the packet level for sensitive PHI fields? Can you do DPI to scrub PII before it leaves the host?
[07:44] Maya: DPI at scale is heavy. We recommend application-level redaction hooks that mask PII before logs or telemetry leaves the environment. For packet-level controls we can integrate with your NGFW to block suspicious flows but redaction should be pre-export.
[07:59] Elena: Any recommendations for SIEM integration? We run Splunk on-prem and want to ingest audit logs with guaranteed ordering and HMAC for integrity.
[08:07] Maya: We'll provide a splunk-forwarder config for reliable delivery, and you can enable signed log exports (HMAC) from the agent before forwarding. We'll include examples in the bundle.
[08:20] Alex: Quick check on data residency — Elena, you mentioned EU-only for some datasets?
[08:27] Elena: Correct. Certain patient records must never leave EU boundaries. For those workloads we need a model serving instance physically located in FRA or on-prem. No replication to us-west.
[08:37] Maya: We can pin model versions to region and prevent cross-region fallback. Our routing can be set policy-based so requests for EU-scope data only route to FRA or on-prem nodes.
[08:48] Samir: But we might want to burst to cloud for compute; how do we reconcile that with residency?
[08:55] Alex: Two options: 1) proxy anonymized/aggregated requests to cloud, 2) use remote execution with encrypted payloads and ephemeral keys held in FRA HSM — more complicated but possible. We'll sketch both tradeoffs in the follow up doc.
[09:07] Maya: Also note network egress must be whitelisted per region. We can help enumerate the endpoints and static IPs for your firewall team.
[09:18] Priya: On the topic of rate limiting and DoS — if inference becomes a target, do you offer rate-limiting per tenant/route?
[09:26] Maya: Yes, per-route quotas and token-bucket enforcement in the edge layer. For Private we can run rate enforcement in your VPC so rules are enforced locally.
[09:35] Elena: For legal/procurement purposes, we need a matrix: who has admin-level access, where keys are stored, and which logs are immutable.
[09:44] Alex: We'll provide an access matrix template. Admin roles are configurable; by default we recommend least privilege with emergency break-glass that requires multi-party approval. Immutable logs can be written to WORM storage in your account.
[09:58] (small cross talk)
[10:10] Samir: A technical nit — how do you handle KV cache eviction to avoid leaking sensitive context?
[10:17] Maya: KV caches are ephemeral in memory and we expose configuration for TTL and forced purge after sensitive sessions. We can also disable caching for specific routes.
[10:27] Priya: Does Redwood support FIPS endpoints for crypto?
[10:31] Maya: We do for our enterprise builds: FIPS-validated crypto libraries and FIPS endpoints on demand. Not all cloud KMS are FIPS by default but you can enable FIPS mode in your account.
[10:42] Elena: For onboarding, the security team will want a runbook that includes: network diagram, firewall rules, key rotation schedule, incident response playbook, and a validation checklist.
[10:51] Alex: Yep, that will be in the compliance bundle. We'll include an onboarding checklist tailored to Lodestar's hybrid topology.
[11:02] Maya: Quick demo of a sample connection flow (described, not live): client in EU hits private endpoint -> VPC endpoint -> internal load balancer -> inference host in FRA VPC, no public IPs, logs forwarded to splunk.
[11:20] Priya: Sounds right. One last question on patching — how do we apply security patches to model-serving hosts in air-gapped env?
[11:28] Maya: We provide signed images and a release manifest. Ops pulls the signed image into air-gapped registry; signature verification happens locally. We'll add a verification script to the repo.
[11:40] Samir: Any known limitations around GPU drivers? We run mixed Ampere and older gen cards in production.
[11:46] Maya: There are kernel and driver compat constraints; our on-prem package includes a compatibility matrix. We also provide a small compatibility shim for older drivers but recommend uniform driver baseline for supported optimizations.
[11:58] Elena: OK — from compliance we also want a sample privacy impact assessment for model training/serving.
[12:05] Alex: We'll include a starter PIA template.
[12:13] (wrap-up)
[12:20] Alex: To recap — Redwood to share: private deployment network diagram, SOC2/ISO bundle, KMS/HSM integration notes, Splunk forwarder configuration, and sample runbooks. Lodestar to share: definitive data residency list, existing network diagrams, and preferred maintenance window. We'll schedule the on-prem lab the week of 9/21.
[12:40] Priya: Thanks everyone. Appreciate the thoroughness, we'll review the docs and get the infra team to work with Maya on runbook details.
[12:50] Maya: Thanks, I'll send the links and the draft runbook after the call.
[12:58] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard terms (e.g., "K V cache" vs "KV cache"), some speaker labels merged where connection dipped. There was light crosstalk during the diagram share around 06:10-06:40.
